question.problem: Consider the equivalence relation $∼$ on the set $A=\{0,1,2,…,9\},$ defined by $a∼b$ if $7∣(b-a).$   How many distinct equivalence classes does $∼$ partition $A$ into?
question.worked_solution:
The equivalence classes of $∼$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a\in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

$$
\begin{aligned}[0] & =\{a\in A\,:\,a∼0\} \\  & =\{a\in A\,:\,7∣(a-0)\} \\  & =\{a\in A\,:\,7∣a\} \\  & =\{0,7\} \\  \\ [1] & =\{a\in A\,:\,a∼1\} \\  & =\{a\in A\,:\,7∣(a-1)\} \\  & =\{1,8\} \\  \\ [2] & =\{a\in A\,:\,a∼2\} \\  & =\{a\in A\,:\,7∣(a-2)\} \\  & =\{2,9\} \\  \\ [3] & =\{a\in A\,:\,a∼3\} \\  & =\{a\in A\,:\,7∣(a-3)\} \\  & =\{3\} \\  \\ [4] & =\{a\in A\,:\,a∼4\} \\  & =\{a\in A\,:\,7∣(a-4)\} \\  & =\{4\} \\  \\ [5] & =\{a\in A\,:\,a∼5\} \\  & =\{a\in A\,:\,7∣(a-5)\} \\  & =\{5\} \\  \\ [6] & =\{a\in A\,:\,a∼6\} \\  & =\{a\in A\,:\,7∣(a-6)\} \\  & =\{6\} \\ \end{aligned}
$$

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $7$ distinct equivalence classes:

$$
[0]=\{0,7\},\,[1]=\{1,8\},\,[2]=\{2,9\},\,[3]=\{3\}\,[4]=\{4\},\,[5]=\{5\},\,[6]=\{6\}.
$$

Notice that the equivalence classes form a partition of $A,$ as expected.
